plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
plan.contextChunk: This figure plots Archimedes' spiral on a single polar grid across one full turn. The grid is a set of concentric gray circles about the origin crossed by gray radial spokes, with horizontal and vertical axes numbered by integers from -7 to 7 in both directions and tipped with arrowheads. A solid dark navy curve starts at the origin and sweeps counterclockwise, its distance from the center growing steadily as it goes, so the trace forms one open loop that never crosses itself and finishes on the positive horizontal axis at about six units out. Six filled black dots mark sample points along the curve, each tagged with an ordered pair whose two entries are equal: (pi/4, pi/4) just above and right of the origin, (pi/2, pi/2) directly above it near height 1.6, (pi, pi) out to the left at about three units, (5pi/4, 5pi/4) down and to the left, (7pi/4, 7pi/4) down and to the right, and (2pi, 2pi) at the loop's end on the right. Because the radius listed in each pair matches the angle listed beside it, the marked dots let the reader confirm the relation r = theta point by point, and the even widening of the loop between successive crossings of a given direction is what a radius growing in direct proportion to the swept angle looks like.

interactionPlan.concept: Archimedes' spiral r = θ is the polar curve whose radius grows in direct proportion to the swept angle, so every plotted point has coordinates of the form (θ, θ) and each full turn widens the loop by the same amount.
elements: polar grid of concentric gray circles about the origin at integer radii 1 through 7
gray radial spokes from the origin at regular angular intervals
horizontal axis and vertical axis with arrowheads, tick marks, and integer labels from -7 to 7 in both directions
solid dark navy spiral curve starting at the origin, sweeping counterclockwise for one full turn, ending on the positive horizontal axis at about 6.3 units out (never self-crossing)
six filled black sample dots on the curve labeled (π/4, π/4), (π/2, π/2), (π, π), (5π/4, 5π/4), (7π/4, 7π/4), (2π, 2π)
movable point marker driven by the θ slider, with a radius line from the origin to the marker and a readout of (θ, r)
highlighted angle ray for a clicked sample point
highlighted radius circle (the circle of radius r = θ) passing through a clicked sample point

interactions.label: θ (angle swept)
interactions.teaches: At every position along the spiral the point's distance from the origin exactly equals the angle swept so far — r = θ holds point by point, not just at the labeled dots

interactions.label: Trace the spiral
interactions.teaches: The spiral is generated by a radius that rotates counterclockwise at a steady rate while lengthening at a steady rate — the curve is the trail left by its tip

Clicking a labeled dot such as (π, π) lights up its angle ray and its radius circle together, showing that both entries of the polar coordinate are the same number — the angle that locates the ray is also the radius of the circle the point sits on

demo_steps.title: A point on the spiral
demo_steps.narration: Drag θ to π/2: the marker sits directly above the origin at distance ≈ 1.57, and the readout shows r equals θ. The spiral's distance from the center tracks the angle swept.

demo_steps.title: Half a turn
demo_steps.narration: At θ = π the marker crosses the negative horizontal axis at distance ≈ 3.14 — one half-turn out, matching the labeled dot (π, π).

demo_steps.title: One full turn
demo_steps.narration: At θ = 2π the curve ends on the positive horizontal axis at ≈ 6.28, the dot (2π, 2π). The gap between successive crossings of the same direction is a constant 2π, because the radius grew by exactly 2π during one more revolution.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: In r = θ the two numbers in every polar coordinate are identical — the angle swept so far IS the distance from the origin, which is why the loop widens evenly with each turn.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Single polar grid: light gray concentric circles with integer ring spacing, light gray spokes, black axes with arrowheads and integer labels -7 to 7 on all four directions. The spiral is one continuous navy stroke from the origin sweeping counterclockwise, ending near (6.28, 0); it must be drawn so the separation between its inner and outer crossings of any ray is visibly uniform. Six black dots with boxed polar labels placed as in the figure: (π/4, π/4) upper-right near origin, (π/2, π/2) above origin, (π, π) on the left axis, (5π/4, 5π/4) lower-left, (7π/4, 7π/4) lower-right, (2π, 2π) at the right end. Keep angular grid lines, spiral, and labels legible at small size by using thin gray grid strokes against a thicker dark navy curve. The slider's moving marker should show a thin radius line from the origin and a live (θ, r) readout; clicking a sample dot highlights its spoke ray and the matching concentric circle in one accent color.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for theta: the learner drags theta from 0 to 2pi, the point travels along the spiral while the radius readout matches the angle readout, making the relation r = theta visible point by point.
- Animation for tracing the spiral: a rotating radius sweeps counterclockwise and leaves the curve behind as it lengthens, showing that Archimedes' spiral is produced by steady angular motion paired with steadily increasing distance from the origin.
- Click for sample points: the learner clicks a labeled dot such as (pi, pi) or (7pi/4, 7pi/4), its angle ray and matching radius circle highlight together, clarifying why both entries in each plotted polar coordinate are equal.

Notice that the r-values are just the decimal form of the angle measured in radians. We can see them on a graph in the figure.

Archimedes’ spiral

Graph of Archimedes' spiral r=theta over [0,2pi]. Starts at origin and spirals out in one loop counterclockwise. Points (pi/4, pi/4), (pi/2,pi/2), (pi,pi), (5pi/4, 5pi/4), (7pi/4, pi/4), and (2pi, 2pi) are marked.
